name: System R costed join planning
summary: IBM's System R chose how to run a database query by comparing the estimated cost of possible join orders, using catalog statistics about the stored data.
description: Relational SQL planning that enumerates multiway joins by subsets, retains plans for useful output orderings, and estimates access cost using catalog statistics and weighted CPU and input/output terms.
tier_reason: The scoped record is a particular configuration, local witness, trial or material application. Dependence across fields or generations on THIS referent is not established; do not inherit the importance of its broader missing family.
why: SQL let users say what data they wanted without saying how to fetch it, so the system itself had to choose an efficient way to run each query.

events.statement: IBM and external joint-study teams evaluated the multiuser System R database in 1978–79.
events.scope: Experimental multiuser System R at IBM and external joint-study sites in 1978–79.
applications: Relational database queries and inventory or research records
events.population: System R joint-study researchers and external user teams
events.caveats: INGRES authors had already formulated a minimum-cost recurrence and implemented a simpler relation-size choice. The 1981 history reports experimental sites, not a commercial product; the reunion does not date each partner’s individual query. The cost optimizer is part of the documented system configuration, not proof every user query used a particular plan.

evidence.supports: System R’s multiuser optimizer preceded experimental external-site evaluations in 1978–79.
The optimizer combines catalog statistics, estimated CPU/I/O costs and join-order selection.
INGRES had an earlier cost recurrence and an implemented smallest-relation selection rule.
Participants recall Pratt & Whitney engine-parts and Upjohn clinical-research uses.
